title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels
subtitle: Defining the precise meaning of MUST, SHOULD, MAY and other requirement keywords

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how to read the capitalized words MUST, SHOULD and MAY in IETF documents. MUST is an absolute requirement, SHOULD allows exceptions for valid reasons, and MAY marks an optional item. Many RFCs cite it so that these words mean the same thing everywhere.

questions: what does must mean in an rfc
what is the difference between must and should in an rfc
what does may mean in an rfc
do lowercase must and should count in rfcs

tldr.problem: Specifications written in everyday English leave readers guessing whether a rule is mandatory, advisable or optional.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a small set of key words (MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY, plus synonyms such as REQUIRED, SHALL, RECOMMENDED and OPTIONAL) and gives authors a one-sentence phrase to cite it.
tldr.outcome: Authors, implementors and reviewers share one vocabulary for requirement levels, with a warning to use the words sparingly, only for interoperation or to limit harmful behavior.

facts.label: Key words
facts.value: MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY

today: Almost every new IETF specification cites this document, usually through the combined phrase from BCP 14: the key words are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 "when, and only when, they appear in all capitals". RFC 8174 (May 2017) removed the doubt about lowercase "must" and "should". The humorous RFC 6919 proposes extra key words, but they are not part of BCP 14.

hero.subtitle: Defining the precise meaning of MUST, SHOULD, MAY and other requirement keywords

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In many standards track documents, several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents.

RFC 2119 is cited by a very large number of RFCs, many of which include the phrase: "The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119."
sections.plainLanguage: Standards documents use certain words to signal requirements, and they are often capitalized. This document defines how those words must be interpreted in IETF documents. Many RFCs cite it with the phrase that the key words are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

sections.title: Keyword Definitions
sections.content:
MUSTAn absolute requirement of the specification. Synonyms: REQUIRED, SHALL.
MUST NOTAn absolute prohibition of the specification. Synonym: SHALL NOT.
SHOULDThere may exist valid reasons to ignore, but implications must be understood and carefully weighed. Synonym: RECOMMENDED.
SHOULD NOTThere may exist valid reasons when behavior is acceptable, but implications should be understood. Synonym: NOT RECOMMENDED.
MAYAn item is truly optional. One implementation may include it while another may omit it. Synonym: OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: MUST (or REQUIRED, SHALL) is an absolute requirement. MUST NOT (or SHALL NOT) is an absolute prohibition. SHOULD (or RECOMMENDED) means there may be valid reasons to ignore an item, but the implications must be understood and weighed. MAY (or OPTIONAL) means an item is truly optional.

sections.title: Guidance for Use
sections.content:
Authors must exercise care in using these terms. They should only be used where actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm.

MUST and Interop
The RFC says these imperatives must be used with care and sparingly: only where actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm (its example is limiting retransmissions). The RFC adds that these words must not be used to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability.
SHOULD and Judgment
SHOULD allows implementors to exercise judgment.
MAY and Optional Features
When MAY is used, other implementations MUST be prepared to interoperate with implementations that do or do not include the optional feature.

The RFC notes that the force of these words is modified by the requirement level of the document in which they are used, and that ignoring a MUST or SHOULD can have subtle security effects, so authors should explain the security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors should use these terms with care and sparingly. They are for cases where they are required for interoperation, or to limit behavior that could cause harm. They must not be used to impose a particular method on implementors when the method is not needed for interoperability.

sections.title: Usage in RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 2119 itself says only that these words are "often capitalized"; it does not say that lowercase forms lose the special meaning. Writing the key words in ALL CAPITALS is the convention that RFC 8174 later made explicit, and lowercase forms carry their normal English meaning.

Example Usage
Correct (RFC 2119 meaning):
"Implementations MUST support UTF-8 encoding."
"The server SHOULD include a Date header."
"Clients MAY cache the response."

Normal English (no RFC 2119 meaning):
"This must be considered carefully."
"Implementations should work well."
"You may find this useful."

RFC 8174 later clarified that the keywords have RFC 2119 meaning only when they are in ALL CAPITALS. This addressed confusion about mixed-case usage like "Must" or "must".
sections.plainLanguage: By convention, the key words are written in capitals to carry the RFC 2119 meaning, and lowercase words keep their normal English meaning. For example, Implementations MUST support UTF-8 is a requirement, while This must be considered carefully is ordinary English. A later RFC made this convention explicit.
